name: Fluoride avoidance

lead: Fluoride avoidance means filtering tap water and choosing fluoride-free products. In looksmaxxing and wellness circles it is tied to claims that fluoride lowers testosterone or calcifies the pineal gland, so avoiding it is said to support hormones and looks.

Health agencies and dental associations endorse fluoridation for preventing tooth decay. A 2024 US court ruling and some studies have raised questions about IQ at high exposures. Reference sources do not list testosterone effects among documented outcomes, and no trial of fluoride avoidance for appearance was found.

paras: Followers use water filters that remove fluoride, switch to fluoride-free toothpaste, and sometimes avoid other fluoridated products. It is a standing habit with no defined results timeline.
The documented harms of fluoride are dental and skeletal fluorosis from high exposure. Avoiding it also means giving up its cavity-prevention effect, which dental bodies endorse.

angle.text: Followers filter water and choose fluoride-free toothpaste, believing fluoride lowers testosterone and so affects masculine development and looks. Dental fluorosis from high exposure is documented; no study links fluoride to testosterone or appearance.

lead: Fluoride avoidance is the practice of limiting fluoride intake by filtering tap water, choosing fluoride-free toothpaste or skipping fluoridated products. The appearance reasons people give are of two kinds: visible tooth changes, since too much fluoride while teeth form can leave mottled enamel (dental fluorosis), and hormonal claims, in which proponents say fluoride lowers testosterone, calcifies the pineal gland or harms cognition, so that avoiding it supports a more masculine, healthier look.[1][2]

Dental fluorosis is the established, visible effect. Wikipedia describes mild fluorosis as small opaque white patches on enamel, with brown staining and pitting in severe cases; it results from swallowing excess fluoride while teeth are forming, mainly before about age 6, and cosmetic options include bleaching, microabrasion, veneers or crowns.[2] That visible link is why smile-focused people sometimes pay attention to fluoride exposure.

Public health agencies and dental associations endorse community water fluoridation for reducing tooth decay, and describe the main established harm of excess fluoride as dental and skeletal fluorosis.[1][3] Opposition has a long history, and recent debate centres on a possible association between high fluoride exposure and lower childhood IQ.[1] Encyclopedic sources do not list testosterone effects among documented outcomes of fluoridation, and no trial of fluoride avoidance for appearance was found.

paras: People who avoid fluoride typically use filtration systems said to remove it from drinking water, switch to toothpaste without fluoride, and avoid foods, teas and beverages made with fluoridated water. Motivations range from general distrust of water additives to specific beliefs about hormones and the brain.[1]

Wikipedia reports the CDC found about 41 percent of US adolescents had definite fluorosis and 20 percent questionable fluorosis, with about 90 percent of cases mild or very mild; very mild cases rose from 17.2 percent in 1986 to 28.5 percent in 2014. Researchers suspect over-consumption from water, toothpaste and varnishes, and the US Public Health Service lowered its recommended water level to 0.7 ppm in 2015.[2]

Another Wikipedia article reports that at 0.7 ppm about 12 percent of participants had fluorosis of aesthetic concern and about 40 percent had fluorosis of any level, and that fluoride works at the tooth surface by helping remineralise enamel and controlling the rate at which cavities develop.[3]

Water fluoridation was introduced in the United States in 1945; early studies reported large reductions in childhood cavities, and later studies smaller ones as toothpaste became common.[1][3] A 2015 Cochrane review estimated reductions of 35 percent in baby teeth and 26 percent in permanent teeth among children with no other fluoride sources, rated as poor-quality evidence, and found no conclusive research for adults.[3]

Opponents have linked fluoridation to cancer, low IQ and diseases of the thyroid and pineal gland; the Wikipedia overview states there is no scientific evidence tying fluoridation to most of these effects.[1] The WHO, CDC, Health Canada and the American Dental Association support fluoridation, while the European Commission noted no advantage over topical use such as toothpaste.[1] The Netherlands' Supreme Court ruled it unauthorized in 1973, and Denmark and Sweden stopped it in the late 1970s and early 1980s.[1]

Naturally high fluoride concentrations can cause severe dental fluorosis, skeletal fluorosis and weakened bones, and improper overfluoridation caused acute poisoning in Alaska in 1992. The WHO guideline maximum of 1.5 mg/L is set so that fluorosis is minimal.[1]

In September 2024 a US federal judge ruled that fluoridation at current levels posed an unreasonable risk of reduced IQ in children and required the Environmental Protection Agency to respond, a decision cited by opponents. A 2006 US National Research Council report on naturally high fluoride levels recommended lowering the US limit.[1]

No studies found testing fluoride avoidance as a method of improving appearance or raising testosterone. Research on fluoridation concerns tooth decay, fluorosis and, more recently, neurodevelopment.[1][3]
